questions.text: Imagine a card game with 2 colors: A (60% of cards) and B (40% of cards). You draw 10 cards at random. Which strategy maximizes your chances of correctly predicting each draw?
options: Predict A about 6 times out of 10 and B about 4 times out of 10
Alternate between A and B equally
questions.explanation: The optimal strategy is to always predict A (60% success). The 'probability matching' error consists of trying to reproduce the proportions (60/40).

questions.text: A machine produces defective parts 30% of the time and good parts 70% of the time. To guess the state of the next part, which strategy is best?
options: Guess 'defective' 3 times out of 10 and 'good' 7 times out of 10
questions.explanation: Always guessing the most probable option (70%) is optimal. Trying to 'match' the probabilities reduces your success rate.

questions.text: In an urn, there are 80% red marbles and 20% blue marbles. You must predict the color before each draw (with replacement). Which approach gives the best success rate over 100 draws?
options: Predict red 80 times and blue 20 times
questions.explanation: Systematically predicting the most frequent option (red) gives 80% success. Other strategies give lower rates.

questions.text: An exam has 70% easy questions and 30% difficult questions. If you must guess the type of the next question without seeing it, what should you answer?
questions.explanation: Always answering 'easy' maximizes your chances (70% success). It's the optimal strategy in the face of uncertainty.

questions.text: A fair coin (50-50 heads or tails) has just landed on heads five times in a row. For the sixth toss:
options: Tails is more likely to come up
Heads is more likely to come up
Heads and tails are equally likely
questions.explanation: The tosses are independent. The coin has no memory. P(heads) = P(tails) = 50% on each toss, regardless of history.

questions.text: At roulette, red has come up 7 times in a row. Which color is most likely to come up on the next spin?
questions.explanation: Each spin is independent. Past results do not influence future spins. This is the 'gambler's fallacy' error.

questions.text: You roll a fair die. It lands on 6 three consecutive times. On the fourth roll, which face has the highest probability of coming up?
options: All faces have the same probability (1/6)
questions.explanation: The die has no memory. Each roll is independent. All faces have exactly 1/6 chance each time.

questions.text: A couple has 4 daughters. They want a fifth child. What is the probability that it will be a boy?
options: More than 50% (they are 'due' for a boy)
Less than 50% (they tend to have girls)
questions.explanation: Each birth is independent. Previous births do not affect the probability of the next child (~50% boy/girl).

questions.text: A basketball team has lost its last 10 games. For the next game against an equally skilled team, which statement is correct?
options: They are more likely to win (return of luck)
They are less likely to win (negative streak)
The chances are about 50-50 (past games don't change probabilities)
questions.explanation: If the teams are equally skilled, each game is independent. Past defeats do not create a 'debt of luck'.

questions.text: Sophie is 28 years old, dynamic and athletic. She goes jogging every morning. Rank these statements by probability (1 = most probable):
options: Sophie is a nurse AND she runs marathons
questions.explanation: P(nurse) > P(nurse AND marathons) because P(A) > P(A ∩ B) always. Adding a condition reduces probability.

questions.text: Marc likes video games and spends a lot of time on his computer. Rank by probability:
options: Marc is a video game developer
Marc works in IT AND plays on an e-sports team
questions.explanation: P(IT) must be ranked more probable than P(IT AND e-sports). The conjunction is always less probable.

questions.text: Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned about issues of discrimination and social justice. Rank by probability:
options: Linda is active in the feminist movement
Linda is a bank teller AND active in the feminist movement
questions.explanation: Despite the description, P(bank teller) > P(bank teller AND feminist) mathematically. This is the famous 'Linda problem'.

questions.text: Paul reads many history books and often visits museums. Rank by probability:
options: Paul is a history teacher AND author of history books
questions.explanation: P(history teacher) > P(history teacher AND author). Adding a condition always reduces probability.

questions.text: A disease affects 1% of the population. A test detects it with 90% sensitivity (true positive) and has 9% false positives. Your test is positive. What is your probability of being sick?
questions.explanation: Out of 10,000 people: 100 sick (90 detected), 9,900 healthy (891 false positives). P = 90/(90+891) ≈ 9.2%.

questions.text: In a company, 70% of employees are engineers and 30% are managers. John is shy and likes puzzles. Is he more likely to be:
options: Impossible to determine with this information
questions.explanation: Even if the description seems to match engineer stereotypes, the base rate (70%) is already a strong indicator.

questions.text: A lie detector is correct 80% of the time (true+ and true-). In a group where 5% of people lie, the detector indicates 'lie' for someone. What is the probability that this person is actually lying?
questions.explanation: Out of 1,000 people: 50 liars (40 detected), 950 honest (190 false positives). P = 40/(40+190) ≈ 17.4%.

questions.text: A city has 2 hospitals: the large one (45 births/day) and the small one (15 births/day). About 50% of babies are boys, but this varies daily. Over a year, which hospital recorded the most days with >60% boys?
questions.explanation: The small hospital. Small samples have more variance. It's easier to get extremes with 15 observations than with 45.

questions.text: In college basketball, players who excel in their first year tend to perform less well in their second year. What is the best explanation?
options: They become complacent after their success
Opponents study their game and adapt
Extreme performances include luck that doesn't repeat
The pressure of expectations affects their performance
questions.explanation: Regression to the mean. Exceptional performances combine talent AND luck. Luck doesn't persist, so performances return toward the mean.

questions.text: Rule to test: 'If Lyon is on one side of the ticket, then train is on the other side.' You have 4 tickets: [Lyon], [Paris], [Car], [Train]. Which ones should you turn over to verify the rule?
questions.explanation: Lyon (verify that the other side = train) and Car (verify that the other side ≠ Lyon). Train and Paris cannot violate the rule.

questions.text: You're checking the law: 'If a person drinks alcohol, they must be 18 years or older.' 4 people: [Drinking beer], [Drinking juice], [25 years old], [16 years old]. Who should you check?
options: Drinking beer, Drinking juice and 16 years old
questions.explanation: Check [Beer] (age ≥18?) and [16 years old] (drinking alcohol?). The others cannot violate the rule.

questions.text: Rule: 'If a product is organic, it must have certification.' 4 products: [Labeled organic], [Labeled conventional], [With certification], [Without certification]. Which ones should you check?
options: Labeled organic, Labeled conventional and Without certification
questions.explanation: Check [Organic] (does it have certification?) and [Without certification] (is it organic?). The others cannot violate the rule.

questions.text: Company rule: 'If a project exceeds €50,000, it requires director approval.' 4 files: [Budget: €75,000], [Budget: €30,000], [Approved by director], [Not approved]. Which ones should you check?
questions.explanation: Check [€75,000] (approved?) and [Not approved] (budget >€50,000?). Logical structure of the Wason task.

questions.text: Researchers have discovered that teenagers who smoke tend to have lower IQ scores. Does this mean that preventing teens from smoking would increase their IQ?
questions.explanation: Correlation ≠ causation. There may be a confounding variable (stress, socioeconomic environment, etc.).

questions.text: A study shows that people who drink coffee have less heart disease. Should we recommend coffee for heart health?
options: Yes, the correlation proves the protective effect
No, a randomized controlled study is needed
Yes, if the correlation is strong
questions.explanation: A correlation doesn't prove causation. Coffee drinkers may have other healthy habits (exercise, diet).

questions.text: We observe that cities with more firefighters have more serious fires. Should we reduce the number of firefighters?
options: Yes, they seem to cause fires
Yes, if there is a real correlation
questions.explanation: Reverse causality: large cities have more fires, so they hire more firefighters. Firefighters don't cause fires.

questions.text: An unpopular school principal is defended because absenteeism has dropped 12% since their appointment. What evidence would best refute this claim?
options: 40% more absences are reported in surveys than in official records
Common sense says that a principal has little impact on absenteeism
Absenteeism rates in two neighboring cities dropped 18% during the same period
The superintendent had questionable business contacts
questions.explanation: Comparison with a control group (similar cities) shows that the drop is general, not due to the principal.

questions.text: A new teaching technique shows +15% success on exams. How to verify its effectiveness?
options: Compare with a control group that did not receive the new technique
questions.explanation: A control group is essential. Results may have increased for other reasons (exam difficulty, motivation, etc.).

questions.text: A neighborhood installs new streetlights and crime drops 20%. Can we conclude that lighting reduces crime?
options: No, we must compare with similar neighborhoods without new streetlights
Yes, if the drop is sustained over time
questions.explanation: Without a control group, we cannot know if the drop is due to streetlights or a general trend of declining crime.

questions.text: Talia has finger thickening. What information is needed to estimate P(Fustis Digitus Syndrome | thickening)?
options: % of people WITHOUT syndrome who have thickening
% of people WITH syndrome who have thickening
questions.explanation: You need P(symptom|disease) and P(symptom|no disease) to calculate P(disease|symptom) via Bayes.

questions.text: To evaluate P(Mechanical failure | Abnormal vibrations), what do you need?
options: P(Vibrations | Failure) and P(Vibrations | No failure)
Only the base rate of failures
questions.explanation: For Bayes, you need the likelihood ratio: P(evidence|H) and P(evidence|not-H).

questions.text: To test whether a new drug reduces fever, which experiment is best?
options: Give the drug to feverish patients and measure temperature 2h later
Give the drug to one group and a placebo to a control group, double-blind
Ask patients if they feel better after the drug
questions.explanation: Randomized controlled double-blind trial: gold standard for testing causal efficacy.

questions.text: A farmer wants to know if a new fertilizer improves yield. Which method is most rigorous?
options: Use it on all fields and compare with last year
Use it on half of each field (randomly assigned) and compare
Use it on their best fields to maximize the test
Ask other farmers who have used it
questions.explanation: Randomization within the same fields controls for confounding variables (soil, water, sunlight).

questions.text: Data table: Rain+Traffic jams=80 cases, Rain+No traffic jams=20, Nice weather+Traffic jams=40, Nice weather+No traffic jams=60. Does rain cause traffic jams?
options: Yes, 80 cases of rain with traffic jams
questions.explanation: Covariation: P(TJ|Rain) = 80/100 = 80% vs P(TJ|Nice) = 40/100 = 40%. Rain increases the probability of traffic jams.

questions.text: Data: Study+Pass=60, Study+Fail=40, Don't study+Pass=30, Don't study+Fail=70. Does studying help to pass?
options: Yes, 60 cases of passing with study
questions.explanation: Covariation: success rate 60% with study vs 30% without study. Studying doubles the chances of success.

questions.text: Hypothesis: 'All swans are white.' Which observation is most informative?
questions.explanation: Popper's principle of falsification: a single counterexample refutes the hypothesis. A thousand confirmations don't prove it.

questions.text: Theory: 'Stress always causes ulcers.' How to rigorously test it?
options: Look for stressed people with ulcers
Look for stressed people WITHOUT ulcers or people with ulcers WITHOUT stress
Measure stress in people with ulcers
questions.explanation: To falsify, look for counterexamples: stress without ulcer, or ulcer without stress. Confirming is not testing.

questions.text: Argument: 'Vaccines contain chemicals. Chemicals are dangerous. Therefore vaccines are dangerous.' This argument is:
questions.explanation: Weak argument: equivocation on 'chemicals'. Water is a chemical. Dose and context determine toxicity.

questions.text: Argument: '90% of accidents happen within 30 km of home. Therefore driving far from home is safer.' This argument is:
questions.explanation: Weak argument: ignores base rate. We drive much more often near home, so more accidents occur there.

questions.text: A bat and a ball cost €1.10 in total. The bat costs €1 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
questions.explanation: 5 cents. If the ball = 5c, the bat = €1.05 (€1 more), total = €1.10. Intuition suggests 10c, but that would give a total of €1.20.

questions.text: If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long does it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets?
questions.explanation: 5 minutes. Each machine makes 1 widget in 5 minutes. So 100 machines make 100 widgets in 5 minutes (in parallel). Intuition suggests 100 minutes.

questions.text: In a lake, there is a water lily. Each day, its size doubles. It takes 48 days to cover the entire lake. In how many days does it cover half the lake?
questions.explanation: 47 days. If the lake is full on day 48 and the size doubles each day, then on day 47 it is half covered. Intuition suggests 24 days.

questions.text: If it takes one minute to make each cut, how long will it take to cut a 25-foot plank into 25 equal pieces?
questions.explanation: 24 minutes. You need 24 cuts to get 25 pieces (not 25 cuts). Intuition suggests 25 minutes.

questions.text: The number of bacteria in a container doubles every hour. If it takes 32 hours to fill the container, how many hours does it take to fill half of it?
questions.explanation: 31 hours. At hour 31, the container is half full. Then it doubles to be full at hour 32. Intuition suggests 16 hours.

questions.text: If you are in a race and you pass the runner in second position, what position are you in now?
questions.explanation: Second position. You take the place of the one who was 2nd. Intuition suggests 1st position.

questions.text: A farmer has 15 sheep. All but 9 die. How many remain?
questions.explanation: 9 sheep. 'All but 9' means that 9 survive. Intuition often suggests 6 (15-9).

questions.text: In a single-elimination chess tournament with 127 players, how many matches are needed to determine the winner?
questions.explanation: 126 matches. Each match eliminates exactly 1 player. To go from 127 to 1 player, you must eliminate 126 players = 126 matches.

questions.text: In a store, an item costs €100. It is reduced by 50%. The next day, there is an additional 20% discount on the sale price. What is the final price?
questions.explanation: €40. First reduction: €50. Then 20% of €50 = €10 discount → €40. Intuition suggests €30 (50%+20%=70% discount).

questions.text: A book and a pen cost €12. The book costs €10 more than the pen. How much does the pen cost?
questions.explanation: €1. If the pen = €1, the book = €11 (€10 more), total = €12. Intuition suggests €2.

questions.text: If 3 cats catch 3 mice in 3 minutes, how long does it take 100 cats to catch 100 mice?
questions.explanation: 3 minutes. Each cat catches 1 mouse in 3 minutes. So 100 cats catch 100 mice in 3 minutes (in parallel). Intuition suggests 100 minutes.

questions.text: Premise 1: All mammals can walk. Premise 2: Whales are mammals. Conclusion: Whales can walk.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (AAA1). Even if the conclusion is false in reality, it follows logically from the premises. Inconsistent syllogism (validity ≠ believability).

questions.text: Premise 1: All fish are bictodes. Premise 2: No shark is a bictode. Conclusion: No shark is a fish.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (AEE2). The conclusion follows from the premises, even if it is false in reality. Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All flowers need water. Premise 2: Roses need water. Conclusion: Roses are flowers.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). Even if the conclusion is true, it does not follow logically from the premises. Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All precious things are rare. Premise 2: Diamonds are rare. Conclusion: Diamonds are precious.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). Just because all precious things are rare and diamonds are rare doesn't mean they are precious. Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: No reptile has fur. Premise 2: All snakes are reptiles. Conclusion: No snake has fur.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (EAE1). The conclusion follows logically from the premises and is true. Consistent syllogism (validity = believability).

questions.text: Premise 1: All birds can fly. Premise 2: Penguins are birds. Conclusion: Penguins can fly.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (AAA1). The conclusion follows from the premises, even if it is false in reality. Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All metals conduct electricity. Premise 2: Copper conducts electricity. Conclusion: Copper is a metal.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). Even if the conclusion is true, it does not follow from the premises. Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All insects have six legs. Premise 2: Spiders have eight legs. Conclusion: Spiders are not insects.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid. The conclusion follows from the premises and is true. Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All plants are zarbons. Premise 2: All ferns are zarbons. Conclusion: All ferns are plants.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). Even if the conclusion is true, it does not follow logically. Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All carnivores eat meat. Premise 2: Tigers eat meat. Conclusion: Tigers are carnivores.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). Even though it's true that tigers are carnivores, this conclusion does not follow logically from the premises. Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: No mammal lays eggs. Premise 2: Platypuses lay eggs. Conclusion: Platypuses are not mammals.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (EAE2). The conclusion follows from the premises, even if it is false (platypuses are mammals). Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All land vehicles have wheels. Premise 2: Trains have wheels. Conclusion: Trains are land vehicles.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). Although true, the conclusion does not follow logically from the premises. Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All fruits contain vitamins. Premise 2: Oranges are fruits. Conclusion: Oranges contain vitamins.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (AAA1). The conclusion follows from the premises and is true. Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: All politicians are liars. Premise 2: John is a liar. Conclusion: John is a politician.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (AAA2). The conclusion does not follow logically from the premises (there can be liars who are not politicians). Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: No airplane can swim. Premise 2: Helicopters cannot swim. Conclusion: Helicopters are airplanes.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically invalid (EEE2). The conclusion does not follow from the premises. Consistent syllogism.

questions.text: Premise 1: No reptile is warm-blooded. Premise 2: All dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Conclusion: No dinosaur was a reptile.
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises
The conclusion does NOT follow logically from the premises
questions.explanation: Logically valid (EAE2). The conclusion follows from the premises, even if it is scientifically debated. Inconsistent syllogism.

questions.text: Three stacked boxes: [Top: fresh strawberries], [Middle: ?], [Bottom: frozen strawberries]. Fresh strawberries must NOT touch frozen ones. Does a box of fresh strawberries touch a box of frozen strawberries?
questions.explanation: Yes. If Middle = fresh, then Middle touches Bottom (frozen). If Middle = frozen, then Top (fresh) touches Middle. In both cases: violation.

questions.text: Anne is looking at Paul. Paul is looking at Marie. Anne is married. Marie is not married. We don't know if Paul is married. Is a married person looking at an unmarried person?
questions.explanation: Yes. If Paul is married, he is looking at Marie (unmarried). If Paul is not married, Anne (married) is looking at him. In both cases: yes.

questions.text: Three aligned doors: [Door A: open], [Door B: ?], [Door C: closed]. At least two consecutive doors must be in the same state. Is door B open or closed?
questions.explanation: Cannot determine. If B is open: A-B are consecutive and open (OK). If B is closed: B-C are consecutive and closed (OK). Both are possible.

questions.text: Three people: John (tie), Marc (?), Sophie (no tie). Rule: If someone wears a tie, their immediate neighbor does not wear one. Does Marc wear a tie?
questions.explanation: No. If Marc wears a tie, then John (his neighbor) should not wear one (contradiction). So Marc does not wear a tie.

questions.text: A coin is tossed twice. We know that: at least one toss gives Heads. What is the probability that both tosses give Heads?
questions.explanation: 1/3. Possible cases knowing at least one Heads: (H,H), (H,T), (T,H). Only (H,H) satisfies 'both Heads' → 1 case out of 3.

questions.text: Three consecutive numbers whose sum is 18. Is the middle number even or odd?
questions.explanation: Even. If the numbers are n, n+1, n+2, their sum = 3n+3 = 18, so n=5. The numbers are 5, 6, 7. The middle (6) is even.

questions.text: Is the distance from San Francisco to Hawaii greater than 500 miles? In your opinion, what is the exact distance?
questions.explanation: The actual distance is ~2387 miles. If your estimate is <1000, you were influenced by the low anchor (500).

questions.text: Is Mars's orbital period around the Sun greater than 1500 days? In your opinion, what is the exact duration?
questions.explanation: The actual duration is 687 days. If your estimate is >1000, you were influenced by the high anchor (1500).

questions.text: Is Australia's population greater than 10 million inhabitants? In your opinion, what is the exact population?
questions.explanation: Australia has about 26 million inhabitants. If your estimate is <20M, you were influenced by the low anchor (10M).

questions.text: Is the hottest temperature ever recorded on Earth greater than 70°C? In your opinion, what is this temperature?
questions.explanation: The record is 56.7°C (Death Valley, 1913). If your estimate is >60°C, you were influenced by the high anchor (70°C).

questions.text: Is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai taller than 500 meters? In your opinion, what is its exact height?
questions.explanation: The Burj Khalifa is 828 meters tall. If your estimate is <700m, you were influenced by the low anchor (500m).

questions.text: Did the Battle of Waterloo take place before 1750? In what year exactly?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Waterloo dates from 1815. If your estimate is <1800, you were influenced by the low anchor (1750).

questions.text: Is the number of bones in the adult human body greater than 300? Exactly how many are there?
questions.explanation: An adult has 206 bones. If your estimate is >250, you were influenced by the high anchor (300).

questions.text: Is the Nile more than 4000 km long? In your opinion, what is its exact length?
questions.explanation: The Nile is about 6650 km long. If your estimate is <5500km, you were influenced by the low anchor (4000km).

questions.text: The Open Door Policy required that:
options: No nation could claim exclusive trading rights in China
Journalists must be allowed to observe the effects of the Cultural Revolution

questions.text: The Treaty of Westphalia ended:
The Suez Canal connects:
options: The Mediterranean and the Red Sea

questions.text: Martin Luther published his 95 Theses in:
The Battle of Waterloo took place in:
Mount Everest is located in:
World War I began in:
Australia is:
The United States Declaration of Independence dates from:
The Great Wall of China is approximately:
Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the height of the Eiffel Tower?
questions.explanation: The Eiffel Tower is 330 meters tall (with antenna).

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the population of Japan?
questions.explanation: Japan has about 125 million inhabitants.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: In what year did Christopher Columbus discover America?
questions.explanation: Christopher Columbus discovered America in 1492.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the length of the Amazon River?
questions.explanation: The Amazon is approximately 6,400 km long.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: How many elements does the periodic table contain?
questions.explanation: The periodic table contains 118 elements.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the speed of light?
questions.explanation: The speed of light is approximately 300,000 km/s.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the boiling point of water at sea level?
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100°C at sea level.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: How many countries are members of the United Nations?
questions.explanation: The UN has 193 member states.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the Earth-Moon distance?
questions.explanation: The average Earth-Moon distance is 384,400 km.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: In what year did the French Revolution take place?
questions.explanation: The French Revolution began in 1789.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the area of the Sahara?
questions.explanation: The Sahara covers about 9 million km².

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: How many continents are there on Earth?
questions.explanation: There are 7 continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania, South America.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the population of France?
questions.explanation: France has about 67 million inhabitants.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.explanation: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: What is the altitude of Mont Blanc?
questions.explanation: Mont Blanc peaks at 4,809 meters.

questions.text: Give a 90% confidence interval: How many time zones does Russia cover?
questions.explanation: Russia spans 11 time zones.

questions.text: A drug reduces the risk of infection from 40% to 20%. By how many percentage points does the risk decrease?
questions.explanation: 40% - 20% = 20 percentage points. Not to be confused with relative reduction (50%).
